Are women better managers?

Are women better managers? 

It’s a question that sparks strong opinions! Fortunately, AUT Business School’s Associate Professor Rachel Morrison has evidence. She shares her take on leadership, gender, and what’s really happening in the workplace. 

#WorkplaceCulture #WomenInLeadership #Management

Why do managers want their workers to come back to the office? | AUT Modern Work Matters

Welcome to Auckland University of Technology’s (AUT) Research Matters! 🚀 AUT’s Research Matters video series is where AUT academics answer everyday questions about their fields of expertise. Get the answers to those questions you’ve always had – or maybe never knew to ask. 

Have you been encouraged back to the office after a few years of working from home? Have your workplace relationships or productivity been impacted by hybrid working? Rachel Morrison, Associate Professor at AUT Business School, is here to answer your questions about work and wellbeing. 

00:00 Introduction  
00:27 Covid made working from home a reality for many workers, but now there seems to be a move against working from home. Why? 
01:37 What are the pitfalls of hybrid working? 
02:43 If you’re given a choice between working in an office or in an open plan workspace, what do you choose and why? 
03:09 Open plan seems to be the default for most offices. Is it just a way for organisations to save money? 
03:23 Does everyone benefit from hybrid working? 
05:10 I work with my best friend, but it can feel complicated in the office – is this normal? 
06:55 Is hot-desking still a thing? 
07:50 My colleague talks too much and too loudly in our open plan space. What can I do to change this? 
08:30 What are the challenges for neurodivergent employees when it comes to open plan workspaces? 
09:08 Is there evidence that biophilia – having elements of nature in the workplace – actually works? 
09:31 What’s the key to being productive at work? 
10:16 Is it true that women are better managers? 
11:14 I’m a manager of a big, productive, hybrid team. How do I get them to come to work more?

Which is worse: ocean pollution or overfishing?

What’s worse for our oceans: pollution or overfishing? 🌊 

On International Ocean Day, marine biologist Dr Dan Breen unpacks the impact of both and why they’re more connected than you might think. 

Because protecting our oceans means understanding the full picture. 
#InternationalOceanDay #OceanHealth #MarineBiology #OceanConservation

One NZ Warriors experience 4G and 5G coverage in the underground CRL tunnels

🏉📶 The One New Zealand Warriors know a thing or two about gaining metres.
Now Auckland’s mobile and transport network is doing the same.
One New Zealand CEO Jason Paris joined One New Zealand Warriors CEO Cameron George deep inside the City Rail Link tunnels to check out the 4G and 5G coverage now live throughout the underground rail network.
When CRL opens, passengers can keep calling, scrolling and streaming all the way to full-time.

CRL Tunnel Vision May 2026

Tēnā koe,
We’re getting close now - and you can feel it. Behind the scenes things are stepping up a few notches as live emergency exercises get underway across the City Rail Link’s new stations and tunnels. Volunteer passengers are helping bring real-world scenarios to life, from onboard incidents to fire response, as rail teams and emergency services work side-by-side to make sure everything runs exactly as it should when it matters most. It’s all part of making sure that when we open later this year, your journey will be not just smooth and reliable, but a safe one too. We also go above ground with mana whenua artist Pāora Puru who takes us through the story behind the striking new Mercury Lane precinct at the doorstep of Karanga-a-Hape Station. A space rich in meaning, history and design.
Enjoy

Webinar: Updating our 2024 advice on emissions budgets

We're engaging with the public about our work to update our 2024 advice on emissions budgets – and we'd like to hear from you. In this webinar, we discuss how we’re updating our analysis on Aotearoa New Zealand’s fourth emissions budget (2036–2040), due by 31 March 2027.

Sharing your evidence and insights is an opportunity to help inform our advice to the Government on what the level of ambition for the fourth emissions budget should be.

General Manager Robin Campbell and Project Director Rob Carr share the scope, response process, and the information and evidence we’re looking for, followed by Q&A.

Share your input and learn more here: https://haveyoursay.climatecommission.govt.nz/comms-and-engagement/eb4-update-2027

Towards Zero: Driving Canterbury wallaby numbers down outside containment

This video shows the number of wallabies reported vs the actual number of wallabies destroyed outside of the containment area since 1998.  From 2021, the impact of the national programme is evident and something we continue to build on today.

Towards Zero: Strengthening farms, reducing wallabies

How did wallabies spread so far, and what happens when no one steps in? This video reflects on how the removal of coordinated management allowed wallabies to escape control, spreading across thousands of hectares of ideal habitat. Once established, the challenge becomes far more difficult and costly. A new, collaborative approach is changing that story. By working together - landowners, government agencies, conservation groups, and Treaty partners, a moving front has been created to tackle wallabies head-on, with real progress already being made. When responsibility is shared, results follow.

Towards Zero: Moving towards zero wallabies

Awareness is growing, and it’s changing the outcome. As more landowners get on board, wallaby sightings are being reported faster, allowing teams to respond before animals move on. Clear signage and community involvement are strengthening the programme and delivering real results. The benefits are clear on the ground: less competition for feed, healthier stock, and noticeable improvements across the South Waitaki. When everyone’s on the same page, progress follows.

Towards Zero: One team, one goal – zero wallabies

A bold mission with a clear goal: stop the spread of Bennett’s wallabies. From replacing ageing rabbit fences with wallaby‑specific exclusion fencing to deploying thermal drones, helicopters, and expert hunters, this integrated pest management programme is using cutting‑edge technology to protect the landscape. This isn’t just about control - it’s about finding and removing the last wallaby.

Kōrero ā-Mahere: 3D StoryMaps for Kaupapa Māori GIS Mapping

This Ngā Poutama Matawhenua online wānanga introduces practical ways to use Esri StoryMaps to turn maps, photos, data, kōrero, and local knowledge into digital stories.

The session is designed for iwi, hapū, marae, Māori land trusts, kaitiaki, planners, researchers, GIS users, councils, agencies, and others working with Māori place-based data. No expert or technical knowledge is needed.

The wānanga demonstrates how StoryMaps can support kaupapa such as 3D fly-throughs between places, incorporating whenua Māori land blocks, showing change over time across awa, moana, mahinga kai and whenua, and sharing taiao restoration, kaitiakitanga, planting, wetland recovery and monitoring mahi.

Topics covered include StoryMap sidecars for guided 3D fly-throughs, swipe maps for before-and-after change, map tours for sites, paths and areas, photos, captions, credits and alt text, collections for connected StoryMaps, and new StoryMaps tools for presentations and social media posts.

Searching for narcotics | Royal New Zealand Navy

Supervising Customs Officer Nick Sparey, from the New Zealand Customs Service Maritime Group, explains how the Royal New Zealand Navy helps prevent drugs from South America reaching our streets.

Overseas intel alerts Customs to vessels of interest that are transiting through New Zealand ports. Cavities along the hull of a ship are frequently used by criminal organisations to store narcotics for later collection by associated gang members. 

Once berthed, Navy engineers shut the vessel down to ensure the RNZN dive team can begin their hull search safely. While the rest of the vessel undergoes a full inspection by Customs teams, including a drug detector dog unit, a Customs boat and Navy dive supervisor oversee the hull search.

Partnering with Customs strengthens the capabilities of both organisations and improves the safety and wellbeing of communities across New Zealand.

2026 mental health and addiction system performance monitoring report

On 16 June 2026 Te Hiringa Mahara – Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission released its latest ‘report card’ on the state of Aotearoa New Zealand’s mental health and addiction system. 

The System performance monitoring report assesses whether people can get help when they need it, where access is not a barrier, the support received is safe and effective, and that we are seeing improved mental health outcomes for people. 

This 2026 report shows that, while progress has been made overall, it has been inconsistent and the benefits are not reaching people with the highest mental health needs. The system must move faster to meet rising need among young people and Māori. 

Based on our assessment of progress, we have made two new recommendations for improvements. We call on Health New Zealand to publish a national seclusion plan by 2027, outlining the pathway to eliminate seclusion, and to the Ministry of Health to expand the collection of outcomes and experience data from people engaging with mental health and addiction services so we can monitor effectiveness of services.

A recommendation first made in June 2024 has been renewed because this has not been realised: we call to Health New Zealand develops an action plan by June 2027 to meet the needs of Māori and whānau accessing specialist mental health and addiction services.

Renewed effort is required by leaders of the mental health and addiction system across all six shifts to improve system performance and address inequities.

Once berthed, Navy engineers shut the vessel down to ensure the RNZN dive team can begin their hull search safely. While the rest of the vessel undergoes a full inspection by Customs teams, including a drug detector dog unit, a Customs boat and Navy dive supervisor oversee the hull search.

Partnering with Customs strengthens the capabilities of both organisations and improves the safety and wellbeing of communities across New Zealand.

Regional Pest Management Plan review online session recording 30 June 2026

We want to improve pest management in Otago, which is why we're reviewing the Regional Pest Management Plan (RPMP). Watch the recording of the online session to learn more and you can help shape the plan.

What is a regional pest management plan?

A regional pest management plan identifies pests in the region and sets goals to either keep these pests out of Otago, get rid of them, or reduce them. The plan also makes rules for people to follow.

There are many pest species that can impact Otago's environment, communities and economy. Under the current plan 51 species are managed. 

Why is the pest plan being reviewed?

Pest plans are required to be reviewed every ten years. The current pest plan was established by Council in 2019, so it’s about time we took another look at it.

A full review of the pest plan takes time. There is a lot of thinking to do around what we might want to improve and what changes are needed to make a more fit for purpose plan.

The Otago Regional Council will be working with our neighbouring regional councils where possible, to ensure our pest plan is aligned with national and regional priorities and supports a collaborative approach to pest management.


About the Otago Regional Council 

The wellbeing of Otago's communities — now and in the future — is at the heart of what we do. Communities rely on us to be a source of knowledge about the region's environment, to lead environmental management in Otago in partnership with mana whenua, and to collaborate with local councils and others for resilient and sustainable communities. 

We advocate for Otago communities on high-priority issues affecting the region.

He waka hourua tuku iho a Ngahiraka-Mai-Tawhiti i tāraia rā e Tā Hekenukumai Ngāiwi Busby tērā e kawe tonu ana i te mātauranga whakatere tuku iho ā ngā wheinga mā ngā pōkai moana roa, te whakangungu, te whakawhiti ahurea, mā te whakamahi i ngā tikanga whakatere tuku iho.

The Ngahiraka-Mai-Tawhiti crew kōrero about waka voyaging – past, present, and future.

Matariki Herenga Waka, the theme of this year’s celebrations, acknowledges the stories, traditions, and mātauranga carried by waka, and the voyages that bring people together.

Ngahiraka-Mai-Tawhiti is a traditional waka hourua built by Tā Hekenukumai Ngāiwi Busby (Tā Hek Busby) that continues to carry ancestral navigation knowledge through long‑distance voyaging, training, and cultural exchange, using traditional wayfinding practices.

In this special kōrero, the crew of Ngahiraka-Mai-Tawhiti and Te Kura Waka share mātauranga about the revitalisation of waka hourua and reflect on how a new generation of navigators are guiding waka through a changing environment.

Pathways to the Sea Strategy: Fish passage through pump stations

Our Pathways to the Sea strategy won the Supreme Award at the 2026 LGFA Taituarā Local Government Excellence Awards on Thursday night (19 June), after winning the category for Excellence in Environmental Leadership.

The strategy embeds ecological outcomes into infrastructure planning and is grounded in a six year, evidence based research programme undertaken by council staff. 

Senior Freshwater Ecologist Alicia Williams Alicia says Pathways to the Sea was a real passion project for everyone involved.

“Developing this strategy to provide safe downstream passage for tuna (eels) and other native fish through our flood protection infrastructure was something we deeply believed in, and we’re incredibly proud of the positive environmental outcomes it will deliver. 

“Winning this award wouldn’t have been possible without the support of our 14 funding partners, and our iwi and hapū partners across the Waikato.”

Co-funded by 14 partners, the research included testing fish friendly solutions, including new pump technologies, gravity bypasses, electrical deterrents and trap and transfer operations. 

Field tested pumps – including a New Zealand designed retrofit prototype – achieved safe passage rates of between 74 and 100 per cent.

Murray's story – Fieldays 2026

Murray Hutchings has been a possum trapper for over 50 years. It’s a career that’s involved a lot of working by himself in remote parts of the country.
After rolling his quad bike down a steep gully, he was left with seven broken ribs, torn muscles in his back, and a badly damaged shoulder.
He credits his survival to crush protection devices, wearing a helmet and carrying a personal locator beacon.

Jane's story – Fieldays 2026

When Jane Blackburne heard sirens one morning in 2020, she assumed they were for someone else. They weren’t, they were for her husband George, who had crashed his quad bike into a drain and broken his neck in two places.
She says partners of injured people tend to get forgotten about, as the focus is naturally on those who’ve been hurt.
Jane’s story is a reminder that workplace incidents don’t just affect the person injured; they affect whānau, too, with consequences that can last a lifetime.

George's story – Fieldays 2026

Horowhenua farm manager George Thompson didn’t expect a routine morning milking to leave him with a broken neck.
Fatigue, working alone, no helmet, no roll protection, and limited communication meant his story could have ended very differently.
George was lucky. A 4:30am call for help was answered and after a long recovery, he can walk again. He hopes others learn from his story and make safer choices around farm vehicles.
